title: ChatGPT and academic integrity: a case study of assessment vulnerability in biological and environmental sciences
text_snippet: ChatGPT and academic integrity: a case study of assessment vulnerability in biological and environmental sciences This study reveals that current assessments in biological and environmental sciences are highly vulnerable to generative artificial intelligence (AI) misuse, which threatens assessment validity. ChatGPT-4 either outperformed or approximated students in exam-style testing and on some essay assignments but struggled with tasks involving data collection, collaboration, and presentations. The authors recommend redesigning assessments to require deeper reasoning, ethical engagement, and clinical or experimental application, alongside ongoing monitoring of AI capabilities and increased use of in-person exams.

title: Employing causality when teaching physiology: deriving the Wiggers diagram from scratch to build better student understanding of cardiac function
text_snippet: Employing causality when teaching physiology: deriving the Wiggers diagram from scratch to build better student understanding of cardiac function Prediction in physiology is the pinnacle of learning outcomes and depends upon comprehension of the biological, chemical, or physical causal links between mechanistic events. The challenge of creating essential cognitive frameworks within which students can successfully think and reason in physiology is to present complex topics in small logical units that do not exceed the working memory capacity. Here we describe how we would develop a logic-driven explanation using the classical Wiggers diagram.

title: Permission to feel: addressing feeling rules as a prerequisite to emotional intelligence skill development in undergraduate prehealth education
text_snippet: Permission to feel: addressing feeling rules as a prerequisite to emotional intelligence skill development in undergraduate prehealth education The exploration of cultural influences on prehealth students’ emotional expression behavior in education contexts brings awareness to potential targets of cultural reform efforts to increase social and behavioral professional skills development. Feeling rules in undergraduate prehealth education are examined and identified in this study. Results suggest that prehealth students perceive an emotionally unsafe learning environment, which may hinder emotional intelligence development. We advocate for research related to increasing social-emotional learning in prehealth education.

title: Moving beyond check-the-box attendance: a token-based approach to encouraging meaningful UTA session participation
text_snippet: Moving beyond check-the-box attendance: a token-based approach to encouraging meaningful UTA session participation This article describes a future-oriented token system used to encourage meaningful participation in undergraduate teaching assistant (UTA)-led review sessions in a large undergraduate physiology course. Rather than awarding points for attendance, students earned limited-use tokens by actively participating in two sessions. The approach shifted the incentive away from check-the-box attendance and toward proactive help seeking, repeated engagement, and collaborative learning.

title: Participation in a medical academic Olympiad is associated with high intrinsic motivation and positive perceptions of academic outcomes
text_snippet: Participation in a medical academic Olympiad is associated with high intrinsic motivation and positive perceptions of academic outcomes This study provides the first empirical evaluation of a student-led medical Olympiad within undergraduate medical education. By analyzing responses from 677 participants, it demonstrates that such initiatives can foster intrinsic motivation and enhance academic outcomes. Although academic Olympiads are well established in basic education, their use and educational impact in medical training have been largely unexplored. These findings highlight the substantial educational potential of student-driven, competition-based learning environments in medical education.

title: Clerkship faculty perspectives on basic science integration during clinical training: implications for fourth-year physiology elective development
text_snippet: Clerkship faculty perspectives on basic science integration during clinical training: implications for fourth-year physiology elective development This study is among the few to use perspectives of clerkship faculty, those who directly observe students’ clinical reasoning, to evaluate basic science preparedness and integration during clerkships. Faculty reported strong support for basic science relevance but identified gaps in its structured integration and in students’ application of foundational knowledge. Findings highlight high-yield domains for reinforcement and demonstrate broad support for targeted fourth-year physiology electives, offering a data-driven model for strengthening vertical basic science integration.

title: Integrating experimental design and statistics throughout an undergraduate human physiology laboratory course
text_snippet: Integrating experimental design and statistics throughout an undergraduate human physiology laboratory course We describe a model for practicing applied biostatistics in an undergraduate human physiology course. Statistical reasoning is embedded in every activity and assignment. Experiments are aligned with a specific statistical analysis, reinforcing experimental design, hypothesis development, data visualization, and interpretation. Through scaffolding, weekly application, in-class activities, Excel activities, and a capstone project, students practice selecting and justifying statistical analyses in authentic contexts. This framework strengthens quantitative confidence and normalizes statistics as an essential tool.

title: Exploring Careers in Healthcare & Onward (ECHO): a community outreach program to promote health care career interest in K-8 students
text_snippet: Exploring Careers in Healthcare & Onward (ECHO): a community outreach program to promote health care career interest in K-8 students Participation in early career-oriented interventions has the potential to increase health care career interest in elementary and middle school students. By engaging youth from the local community in health care hands-on, career-oriented learning experiences, such programs may be able to empower students from underresourced communities to consider the pursuit of future careers in health care.

title: Incorporating advanced neuroscience research in undergraduate neuroscience education
text_snippet: Incorporating advanced neuroscience research in undergraduate neuroscience education Rapid advances in neuroscience underscore the need to prepare students for a highly competitive academic and research environment. We report specifically designed short-term research projects implemented as practical components of a third-year undergraduate course. Within these projects, students review background literature, collect data, perform analyses, and present findings to address defined scientific questions. These practical components not only provide valuable insights into neuroscientific methods but also reinforce students’ understanding of the fundamental principles of neuroscience.

title: Don’t use Costanzo
text_snippet: Don’t use Costanzo A medical school faculty member deals with the blow dealt by a student’s public, all-caps dismissal of her physiology textbook.

title: A practical approach to estimate the potency of an antagonist in a functional experiment with isolated preparations of rat aorta
text_snippet: A practical approach to estimate the potency of an antagonist in a functional experiment with isolated preparations of rat aorta By utilizing phenylephrine and prazosin in isolated rat aortas, students can better understand the concept of antagonist potency. This activity provides a practical opportunity to discuss key aspects of cell-drug interactions, including efficacy and intrinsic activity, via parameters such as EC 50 , IC 50 , equilibrium dissociation constant ( K b ), and antagonist potency (pA 2 ).

title: Pulse of Surgery: an immersive educational operating room experience for the community
text_snippet: Pulse of Surgery: an immersive educational operating room experience for the community Pulse of Surgery is a unique immersive experiential initiative for students and community members that integrates a live cardiac surgery complemented by real-time bidirectional engagement and discussions with the surgical team and fun hands-on educational activities. Overarching goals are to promote the health care fields, educate participants in strategies for maintaining cardiovascular health, and inspire the next generations to consider a STEM or health care career.

title: Effectiveness of practicing with an e-learning tool based on an error-driven learning algorithm in physiology education
text_snippet: Effectiveness of practicing with an e-learning tool based on an error-driven learning algorithm in physiology education We developed an e-learning tool conceptually based on error-driven learning and implemented it in a first-year physiology course. The tool was designed to support correction of incorrect recall through repeated corrective feedback. Using objective measures derived from student activity logs, we showed that the number of repeated practices was significantly associated with learning improvement and final examination scores, even after adjusting for baseline academic aptitude and initial accuracy. This approach may support introductory physiology education.

title: Effect of a 3-D cell membrane model combined with an interactive online platform on health students’ learning of cellular physiology
text_snippet: Effect of a 3-D cell membrane model combined with an interactive online platform on health students’ learning of cellular physiology Cell membranes are invisible to the naked eye, yet vital to life. For health care students, understanding transport across membranes can be challenging. This study combined a 3-D puzzle model with an online platform to make these processes tangible and easier to grasp. Students who used this interactive approach improved their self-perception of cellular function, showing that playful, hands-on educational strategies can facilitate learning of complex biological concepts and promote greater engagement in the learning process.

title: Interactive visualization of enzyme kinetics: a shiny app for biomedical, pharmacology, and biochemistry education
text_snippet: Interactive visualization of enzyme kinetics: a shiny app for biomedical, pharmacology, and biochemistry education Students often find enzyme kinetics difficult because mathematical models can appear disconnected from biological meaning. The freely available Kinetics Analysis App was created to help address this challenge. Through interactive visualization of four classical kinetic models, learners are able to explore parameter estimation and model selection in real time. This web-based tool supports active learning, improves confidence in data interpretation, and provides an accessible approach for teaching quantitative concepts in biomedical and pharmacological sciences.

title: Revealing the link between critical thinking disposition and learning approaches: a cross-sectional study among Chinese medical students
text_snippet: Revealing the link between critical thinking disposition and learning approaches: a cross-sectional study among Chinese medical students This study is among the first to examine how deep and surface learning approaches predict CT disposition in Chinese medical students. By integrating the R-SPQ-2F and the CTDI-CV, we not only analyzed the associations between CT dispositions and LA but also developed a regression model explaining 39% of CT variance. Our findings highlight that innovative activities and academic performance moderate the CT-LA relationship, suggesting actionable targets for curriculum reform.

title: Goat rib bone marrow thick smear preparation as a low-cost, ethical, and high-utility laboratory exercise for teaching hematopoiesis
text_snippet: Goat rib bone marrow thick smear preparation as a low-cost, ethical, and high-utility laboratory exercise for teaching hematopoiesis The present model introduces an active, hands-on learning approach that moves beyond passive slide-based instruction by directly engaging students in laboratory preparation and microscopic analysis. It establishes a sustainable, low-cost teaching resource for physiology laboratories while effectively bridging theoretical concepts of hematopoiesis with their clinical and morphological correlates. Importantly, the method is scalable and well suited for institutions with limited infrastructure, enabling authentic laboratory-based learning experiences without reliance on scarce human samples.

title: Project-based learning to promote multidisciplinary integration and transferable skills in undergraduate biology students
text_snippet: Project-based learning to promote multidisciplinary integration and transferable skills in undergraduate biology students How can we break down disciplinary silos in biology? This study presents a project-based learning model implemented over 3 yr with 675 students. By exploring concrete and authentic research topics, students combine multidisciplinary investigation with the development of key transferable skills including teamwork, scientific communication, and autonomy. A practical guide to transforming biology education and better preparing future physiologists for interdisciplinary challenges.

title: ECGSight: a digital caliper application for teaching electrocardiogram interpretation in undergraduate medical education
text_snippet: ECGSight: a digital caliper application for teaching electrocardiogram interpretation in undergraduate medical education ECGSight is an open-source, interactive digital caliper application developed with R and Shiny for measuring ECG segments and intervals from digital ECG images. It restores active, measurement-based learning that is often lost when students rely on automated ECG interpretations on screens. By shifting ECG education from passive viewing to deliberate skill engagement, the tool helps students better understand ECG scaling, interval boundaries, and clinical variability in a digital environment.

title: “Gastrointestinal Circuit”: an active learning approach to enhance understanding of human digestive system physiology
text_snippet: “Gastrointestinal Circuit”: an active learning approach to enhance understanding of human digestive system physiology Physiology education often faces challenges such as limited instructional time, complex content, and low student engagement, leading to high failure rates. This study introduces the “Gastrointestinal Circuit,” a low-cost, active learning activity using large visual materials and interactive tasks to enhance undergraduate teaching of gastrointestinal physiology. Seventy students from Nursing, Speech-Language Pathology, and Biological Sciences participated in a pretest-posttest design and opinion survey. Results showed significant learning gains (P ≤ 0.05), particularly in the areas of gastrointestinal hormones and the enteric nervous system, as well as high student satisfaction. Additionally, the 2023 cohort, which participated in the “Gastrointestinal Circuit” activity, outperformed the 2022 cohort, which received only traditional lecture-based instruction, on related exam questions (P = 0.0035). These findings suggest that the “Gastrointestinal Circuit” is an effective and engaging tool for improving physiology education, with potential for further refinement.

title: Bridging basic physiology and clinical reasoning: student perceptions of a case-based collaborative activity with AI support
text_snippet: Bridging basic physiology and clinical reasoning: student perceptions of a case-based collaborative activity with AI support This study describes a simple, reproducible case-based collaborative activity in an introductory undergraduate physiology course in which students were permitted to use AI tools while solving clinical problems involving membrane transport disorders. The activity was associated with stronger perceived links between membrane transport and disease, greater confidence in mechanistic explanation, and continued reliance on peer discussion for deeper understanding. These findings suggest that AI can support, but should not replace, collaborative learning in physiology education.

title: JANATO: a comprehensive approach to exploring anatomy learning experiences and academic development in undergraduate and graduate education in Brazil
text_snippet: JANATO: a comprehensive approach to exploring anatomy learning experiences and academic development in undergraduate and graduate education in Brazil This study presents JANATO, an anatomy course integrating theory, applied anatomy, human tissue dissection, and research experiences to address persistent challenges in anatomy education. By combining participant evaluations with a SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats) analysis from organizers, the study offers a dual-perspective assessment. JANATO enhances learner engagement while supporting academic and professional development among organizers. The results identify actionable improvements and can serve as a model for anatomy and related disciplines for training future clinicians and educators.

title: A flipped physiology course positively impacted student success and perceptions of learning
text_snippet: A flipped physiology course positively impacted student success and perceptions of learning Utilizing the frameworks of Bloom’s Taxonomy and Constructivism, a flipped classroom in physiology showed an increase in the percentage of passing grades compared to traditional pedagogy, and students demonstrated the ability to use prior knowledge on a novel task. Their satisfaction with the flipped pedagogy was mixed, but this was primarily due to factors such as video quality and test modality (which was not unique to the flipped classroom).

title: Engaging the powerhouse: mitochondrial biology learning through Minecraft
text_snippet: Engaging the powerhouse: mitochondrial biology learning through Minecraft The Minecraft Mitochondrial World (MMW) is the first comprehensive tertiary-level cell biology learning environment developed in Minecraft Education Edition (MEE). We describe an innovative approach to designing and deploying a dynamic, interactive, and experiential mitochondrial learning experience in MEE. The approach includes sophisticated simulations to model cellular respiration. We further describe how the MMW’s design principles make complex mitochondrial biology engaging, understandable, and enjoyable for learners of diverse educational backgrounds and learning preferences.

title: A storytelling approach to type 1 diabetes mellitus community health education to promote early recognition in underserved populations
text_snippet: A storytelling approach to type 1 diabetes mellitus community health education to promote early recognition in underserved populations This study addresses a critical gap in type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) education by focusing on early symptom recognition rather than disease management after diagnosis. Using a storytelling-based community intervention, we demonstrated significant improvements in knowledge, awareness, and confidence among adults in underserved populations. Notably, no prior studies have evaluated storytelling to promote earlier identification of T1DM. These findings highlight an innovative, scalable approach to reduce delayed diagnosis and prevent life-threatening complications such as diabetic ketoacidosis.

title: Cellular and network mechanisms of spreading depolarization
text_snippet: Cellular and network mechanisms of spreading depolarization This Staying Current article details the fundamental mechanisms of spreading depolarization (SD), a common central nervous system phenomenon rarely discussed in neuroscience curricula that is implicated in many neuropathologies, including mild and traumatic brain injury, migraine, and stroke. Therefore, incorporating SD into neuroscience education adds clinically relevant context that engages students and supports deeper understanding of foundational neurophysiology.

title: Public health frameworks increase student’s ability to propose solutions addressing health inequity
text_snippet: Public health frameworks increase student’s ability to propose solutions addressing health inequity The present study finds that teaching methods from public health disciplines in the physiology classroom improve students’ understanding of how to develop ideas to reduce cardiovascular disease (CVD) inequities. Our data support the notion that a multidisciplinary approach on the part of the instructor, integrating disciplinary knowledge from outside of physiology, is an effective approach to enhance problem-solving skills regarding CVD in marginalized populations.

title: Exploring qualitative education research: a primer for physiologists
text_snippet: Exploring qualitative education research: a primer for physiologists Predicting student outcomes only tells half of the learning story. To fully understand student learning, we must also understand their experience. This guide aims to demystify qualitative education research. From foundational theory to real-world examples, learn how to capture the “why” of student learning.

title: Diagnostic instruments in extended curriculum programs: a scoping review
text_snippet: Diagnostic instruments in extended curriculum programs: a scoping review We propose a framework for diagnostic instrument development that incorporates cultural appropriateness, to ensure that the instrument respects and aligns with cultural norms; contextual relevance, ensuring that the instrument is suitable for specific situations; persistence, which evaluates students’ ability to continue despite challenges; psychosocial skills, which assesses social and emotional competencies; life skills, which measures practical abilities needed for daily life; content knowledge, which evaluates understanding of specific subjects; and cognitive abilities, which assesses cognitive abilities.

title: BioQueer : educational narratives on sex and gender—a methodology for developing, implementing, and evaluating an instructional guidebook
text_snippet: BioQueer : educational narratives on sex and gender—a methodology for developing, implementing, and evaluating an instructional guidebook This study evaluates the BioQueer guidebook, an educational intervention developed to improve undergraduate understanding of differences of sex development (DSD) and sex and gender concepts. With a one-group pretest-posttest design with ordinal analysis [cumulative link model (CLM)], results showed consistent increases in participant scores. Despite design limitations, findings support the guidebook’s clarity and pedagogical potential. This exploratory study informs future research, including a planned randomized controlled trial to assess causal effects in physiology education.

title: Designing a human-AI collaborative model for precision teaching in undergraduate physiology laboratory education: a modified Delphi study
text_snippet: Designing a human-AI collaborative model for precision teaching in undergraduate physiology laboratory education: a modified Delphi study This study develops a human-AI collaborative precision teaching framework for undergraduate physiology labs with a four-module model. Through a two-round modified Delphi study with 15 experts, the study established consensus on scientific validity, feasibility, phased AI implementation, teacher leadership, ethical safeguards, knowledge graphs, and targeted training. The framework offers a practical, ethically grounded roadmap integrating AI while preserving teacher agency, pedagogical integrity, and equitable student support.

title: Unraveling the enigma of digestion: a digital educational activity as a tool for teaching digestive system physiology
text_snippet: Unraveling the enigma of digestion: a digital educational activity as a tool for teaching digestive system physiology We present a novel teaching approach in the form of an innovative digital marathon that integrates active learning strategies with widely accessible social media platforms to support the remote teaching of digestive system physiology. This approach illustrates how interactive, low-cost digital tools can be structured to facilitate engagement and discussion of theoretical content in virtual or hybrid learning environments.

title: Countercurrent multiplication revisited: key conceptual updates and framework expansion
text_snippet: Countercurrent multiplication revisited: key conceptual updates and framework expansion This article makes three advances in renal osmoregulation education and research. It provides a classroom-ready diagram to teach the emergence of the corticopapillary osmotic gradient and refines key countercurrent multiplication (CCM) concepts from my prior work. It reframes the transepithelial osmotic difference (ΔOC) as a system-level parameter amplified cycle by cycle during CCM. It also expands the CCM–equilibrium renal osmoregulation framework by reconceptualizing renal osmoregulation as a more dynamic, physiologically plausible operating regime punctuated by CCM episodes.

title: GutDigest: a new game to enhance active learning and assessment of gastrointestinal digestion of macromolecules
text_snippet: GutDigest: a new game to enhance active learning and assessment of gastrointestinal digestion of macromolecules We describe the development of GutDigest, a new online educational game, to enhance the teaching, learning, and assessment of macromolecular digestion, which is a complex topic in gastrointestinal physiology courses across various curricula of medical and health science programs globally. The game will be a useful revision resource for students and an assessment tool for tutors to gauge their knowledge after being exposed to preliminary teaching of the topic.

title: Physiology of menopause and the role of hormone therapy
text_snippet: Physiology of menopause and the role of hormone therapy Natural menopause remains underrepresented in medical curricula, leaving clinicians with gaps in reproductive-aging knowledge. This Staying Current article gives physiology educators an updated, evidence-based overview—covering hormonal regulation, STRAW/STRAW + 10 staging criteria, and the pathophysiology of vasomotor, genitourinary, mood, and sleep symptoms. It critically revisits menopausal hormone therapy, including lessons from the Women's Health Initiative, alongside nonhormonal alternatives, equipping instructors to strengthen curricula and advance patient-centered women's health care.

title: The creation of freely accessible cardiac physiology and anatomy educational tools: AR, VR, mobile applications, and the Atlas of Human Cardiac Anatomy website
text_snippet: The creation of freely accessible cardiac physiology and anatomy educational tools: AR, VR, mobile applications, and the Atlas of Human Cardiac Anatomy website This article presents a suite of free mobile, augmented reality (AR), and virtual reality (VR) applications developed by the Visible Heart Laboratories at the University of Minnesota. These applications leverage real human heart anatomical data and advanced three-dimensional (3-D) imaging to provide immersive simulations that enhance learning for students and professionals worldwide. Designed for broad accessibilities, these applications allow users to explore the intricacies of detailed cardiac anatomy in highly interactive formats including mobile devices and AR/VR platforms.

title: Teaching Contemporary Lactate Physiology: Why It Is Time to Retire “Lactic Acid”
text_snippet: Teaching Contemporary Lactate Physiology: Why It Is Time to Retire “Lactic Acid” The terminology used to teach physiology should reflect contemporary scientific understanding. Although decades of research have fundamentally transformed our understanding of lactate biology, the term lactic acid remains widely used throughout physiology education, textbooks, coaching education, certification programs, and public communication. Under physiological conditions, however, lactate—not lactic acid—is the predominant molecular species, and modern evidence recognizes lactate as an oxidative fuel, signaling molecule, and regulator of metabolism rather than a metabolic waste product. This Perspective argues that physiology education should preferentially adopt terminology consistent with contemporary lactate biology. We discuss the historical origins of the term lactic acid, summarize the scientific advances that have reshaped our understanding of lactate physiology, and propose a practical educational framework for communicating these concepts across diverse learning environments. title: Amino Acid—Who R You? An interactive browser-based game for learning amino acid properties
text_snippet: Amino Acid—Who R You? An interactive browser-based game for learning amino acid properties Connecting amino acid side-chain properties to protein structure and physiological function is foundational, yet physiology and biomedical science students have uneven chemistry backgrounds, and this knowledge is often assumed rather than revisited. We developed Amino Acid—Who R You?, a browser-based game for scalable, low-stakes practice. Across three modes, learners identify a hidden residue through yes-or-no questions, classify residues using cumulative clues, or retrieve full names from codes and structures. Adjustable visual, textual and symbolic cues allow learners to vary support while practicing the same chemistry. Requiring no installation or account, the resource was introduced in a lecture after amino acid structures and properties were taught, then made available through the virtual learning environment for independent study. It aims to consolidate this chemistry for reasoning about enzyme catalysis, receptor binding, ion-channel gating and membrane transport. We describe its rationale, mechanics, implementation and limitations.

title: Making the First Home-Trained Physiologists in Rwanda: An Experiential Narrative of Lessons Learned while Designing and Implementing the MSc Physiology Program
text_snippet: Making the First Home-Trained Physiologists in Rwanda: An Experiential Narrative of Lessons Learned while Designing and Implementing the MSc Physiology Program Before 2023, Rwanda did not have a Physiology training program. This study aimed to describe the approved curriculum of the program at the University of Rwanda (UR) and gather the perceptions of students and lecturers on the implementation of the first-ever physiology training in Rwanda. This experiential qualitative study adopted a narrative phenomenological approach to describe the retrospective events. The first objective was achieved by content analysis of the approved program documents, while objective 2 involved an informal survey as part of the University’s quality assurance policy. The questions and their responses were related to the students’ inspiration to study Physiology at the M.Sc. level, robustness of the curriculum content and its associated academic stress, teaching effectiveness by the lecturers, assessment strategies, comparison of the level of difficulty with other programs in the University, ability of the graduates to compete with others trained elsewhere, preparation for an academic research career, strengths of the program that should be sustained, and weaknesses of the program that should be abolished or adjusted. title: Impact of Cardiovascular Disease and Health Disparities in the Obstetric Population
text_snippet: Impact of Cardiovascular Disease and Health Disparities in the Obstetric Population Pregnant individuals represent a uniquely vulnerable population, as the physiologic demands of pregnancy can unmask or worsen underlying conditions while simultaneously influencing fetal development. Building on prior discussions of cardiovascular adaptation during pregnancy, this review examines maternal and fetal health through a public health lens, emphasizing how social determinants of health shape obstetric outcomes. Although normal cardiovascular changes promote fetal growth, these shifts can exacerbate undiagnosed or poorly controlled conditions, leading to higher rates of complications. Research consistently shows that these negative outcomes are not equitably distributed. Significant disparities exist across racial and ethnic groups, reflected in metrics such as preterm birth, maternal morbidity, and cardiovascular complications. African American, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and American Indian or Alaska Native populations experience markedly higher rates of adverse outcomes compared with White counterparts. title: Addressing the Public Health Risks of Caffeinated Alcoholic Beverages Through Brief Health Education
text_snippet: Addressing the Public Health Risks of Caffeinated Alcoholic Beverages Through Brief Health Education The combined use of caffeine and alcohol, commonly referred to as caffeinated alcoholic beverages (CABs), is prevalent among young adults and is associated with increased alcohol consumption, reduced perception of intoxication, and higher-risk behaviors such as binge drinking and impaired driving. Despite these risks, gaps remain in public knowledge regarding the health consequences of combining these substances. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate whether a brief educational intervention could improve knowledge of the risks associated with CAB consumption and increase willingness to reduce CAB use. An interactive educational intervention covering the prevalence of CAB consumption among young adults as well as its effects and risks was developed. The educational intervention was delivered as either a group presentation or condensed one-on-one sessions. Participants completed pre- and post-intervention surveys assessing knowledge and attitudes toward CAB use. A paired t-test was used to compare mean knowledge scores before and after the intervention. Of the 118 individuals who participated, 94 completed both surveys and were included in the analysis. title: Enhancing Learning, Teamwork, and Communication: Crime Scene Investigation Murder Board Integrated into Lab Activities
text_snippet: Enhancing Learning, Teamwork, and Communication: Crime Scene Investigation Murder Board Integrated into Lab Activities Moving from the sage on the stage while lecturing to active learning has been a common pedagogical shift for many years. Yet laboratory sections which are co-requisite courses with the lecture often remain unchanged. The laboratory experiment follows a standard design, often called the cookbook method, of creating a hypothesis, running the experiment, analyzing data, and drawing conclusions. Yet this design has little student exchange of ideas or active discussion. In our study, we revised a three-week crime scene investigation (CSI) laboratory module by adding a murder board. The murder board, a large bulletin board, served as the landing place for victim and suspect biographies. Students added each of the four suspects’ motives, means, opportunity, and alibis. Each week students performed laboratory experiments, blood typing, ELISA for HIV, DNA fingerprinting, to gather evidence to identify the murderer. The weekly data was added to their murder boards followed by robust, enthusiastic, and energetic discussion as students eliminated suspects and recreated hypotheses. To assess student learning, teamwork, and engagement, a survey was given after the laboratory module was completed

title: The Reverse Native-Speaker Problem: Teaching Physiology to a Generation Fluent in Tools We Are Still Learning
text_snippet: The Reverse Native-Speaker Problem: Teaching Physiology to a Generation Fluent in Tools We Are Still Learning Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping physiology education, but the central challenge is epistemic, not technological. Learners are often more fluent with AI tools than their instructors, yet less fluent in the physiology those tools describe: a pattern this Perspective terms the reverse native-speaker problem. AI-generated explanations of physiological mechanisms are rarely overtly wrong. An interpretive framework proposed by means of this perspective states that explanations that appear plausible step by step may become become inconsistent when organ systems are considered together. It is therefore argued that the educator role is shifting from transmitting information to certifying coherence and proposes a classroom exercise, the error-hunt, for identifying seeded, systems-level inconsistencies in AI-generated explanations.

title: More than marks: The Broader Educational Contribution of Generative AI in Biomedical Science
text_snippet: More than marks: The Broader Educational Contribution of Generative AI in Biomedical Science In higher education, discussion surrounding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) often centers on academic integrity and potential grade inflation. However, much less attention has been given to how GenAI may be reshaping the learning process itself, including how students reason and construct understanding. This gap limits our ability to evaluate GenAI in educational terms that extend beyond performance outcomes. This study examined the association between declared GenAI use and academic performance in undergraduate biomedical science courses, using physiology and biochemistry as disciplinary contexts. Student grades were analyzed between declared GenAI Users and Non-users within each course and across assignments. Contrary to common assumptions that using GenAI would advantage or disadvantage students academically, no measurable difference in performance was observed between Users and Non-users in any analysis. This consistent absence of a grade effect occurred alongside evidence that students primarily declared using GenAI for tasks such as concept explanation rather than core content generation. title: A Comparison of Game-Based Learning and Peer-Assisted Learning in Cardiovascular Physiology among First-Year Medical Students: A Randomized Controlled Crossover Trial
text_snippet: A Comparison of Game-Based Learning and Peer-Assisted Learning in Cardiovascular Physiology among First-Year Medical Students: A Randomized Controlled Crossover Trial Direct comparisons between game-based learning and peer-assisted learning (PAL) in cardiovascular physiology remain limited despite growing emphasis on active learning in medical education. This randomized controlled crossover trial compared a novel educational board game, CardioLeague (Group A), with PAL (Group B) among first-year MBBS students. Thirty-six students who had completed cardiovascular physiology lectures were randomized 1:1 into two groups (n = 18 each). Knowledge was assessed via multiple-choice questionnaire at pre-test, immediately after intervention (post-test 1), one week later (post-test 2), and after crossover to the alternate method (post-test 3). Four participants in Group A and two in Group B were lost to follow-up before post-test 2 (n = 30 thereafter). Learner perception was assessed with an 18-item Likert-scale questionnaire (Cronbach’s α = 0.960). Both groups showed significant within-group knowledge gains after their initial intervention (Group A: 13.39 ± 4.82 to 16.56 ± 4.05, P = 0.0024**; Group B: 15.17 ± 5.73 to 17.83 ± 4.74, P = 0.0236*), with no significant between-group difference at any assessment point (all P > 0.05; Cohen’s d = −0.29 to 0.22).

title: Active recall of scientific methodology principles improves performance in the Investigating Human Physiology smartphone-assisted experimentation activity
text_snippet: Active recall of scientific methodology principles improves performance in the Investigating Human Physiology smartphone-assisted experimentation activity The "Investigating Human Physiology" (IHP) activity is an inquiry-based instructional strategy for first-year Science Education students, in which students select smartphone applications that monitor physiological variables and body signs, and test a hypothesis through smartphone-assisted experimentation, before receiving formal instruction in scientific methodology. We investigated whether prior exposure to scientific methodology is a prerequisite for success in the IHP and whether the format of supplementary methodology instruction affects performance. Students (N = 169) received the standard IHP instructions and were assigned to control (CTL, no supplementary material), active recall questions upon reading of a text (TXT, a written text followed by 11 digital flashcards in a question and answer format), and video (VID, passive audiovisual material) groups. Reports were scored with a validated rubric and categorized by physiology topic and variable. TXT scored significantly higher than CTL overall (p = 0.037) and on hypothesis clarity (p = 0.046), theoretical grounding (p = 0.034), prediction (p = 0.001), and conclusion (p = 0.009); methodology and results criteria did not differ

title: Acid alone does not digest: a lesson from nineteenth-century stomach physiology
text_snippet: Acid alone does not digest: a lesson from nineteenth-century stomach physiology "Gastric acid" and "gastric juice" are commonly used as interchangeable terms, thus obscuring a distinction that took physiologists generations to establish. Hydrochloric acid denatures dietary protein, activates pepsinogen, and maintains the pH at which pepsin is active – but it does not itself hydrolyze peptide bonds (i.e., digest). Disentangling the interplay between acid and pepsin required independent, near-simultaneous work in Germany and the United States in the early 1830s, followed by Theodor Schwann's isolation, in 1836, of a separate heat-sensitive agent he named pepsin. The elimination logic Schwann used to reach that conclusion – testing and ruling out each plausible alternative in turn – offers a reasoning model still worth teaching today.

title: What tips the balance? Reflections on a Responsible Conduct of Research Course
text_snippet: What tips the balance? Reflections on a Responsible Conduct of Research Course Graduate education in the sciences often emphasizes technical skills, yet ethical reasoning is equally essential to the integrity of research. This article reflects on more than a decade of teaching research ethics to graduate students in physiology and other disciplines. I used ambiguous scenarios, encouraged peer discussion, and designed an assignment that engaged students with real-world policy. Several of these scenarios flip the script in that there may be cases where it is more ethical to discard data and where authorship is appropriate even if the author’s sole “contribution” was to remove information from the paper. By embracing ambiguity, engaging students in real dilemmas, and encouraging them to reflect on policies and expectations, I tried to equip the students to not only to comply with regulations but to shape the culture of science with integrity.
